sentences.text: Mymoorapelta is one of the smaller nodosaurids, with the largest known specimen estimated at 3 meters long, yet a large portion of its postcranial skeleton has been discovered.
The animal possessed a narrow snout and an almost triangular skull featuring two large backward-pointing horns from the brow and two additional horns pointing backward and downward from the jugal.
Its neck vertebrae have centra that are wider than tall with a heart-shaped morphology, while the body was characterized by large spiked osteoderms protruding from the sides and back.
The genus is known from portions of a disarticulated skull, parts of three different skeletons, and other postcranial elements.
This species stands out as one of the smaller nodosaurids, with the largest known individual reaching only 3 meters in length.
Unlike club-tailed ankylosaurids, Mymoorapelta had a tail with spikes likely used for defense.
Fossils of Mymoorapelta and Allosaurus preserving bite marks were described by Stephanie Drumheller et al. in 2020.
James Kirkland and Kenneth Carpenter initially described Mymoorapelta in 1994.
Fossils were first discovered in the Mygatt-Moore Quarry in 1990, which dates between 151.89 and 152.47 million years ago.
A new Mymoorapelta specimen was unearthed at the Hanksville-Burpee Quarry near Hanksville, Utah, and mentioned in a 2015 abstract.
Mymoorapelta was a low browser that fed on cycads and conifers, utilizing a narrow snout as an adaptation for selective browsing rather than grazing.
Nodosaurid teeth, including those of Mymoorapelta, were blade-like, larger, and more complex than ankylosaurid teeth, featuring rough enamel and a crenelated cingulum.

Evidence from related ankylosaurs suggests Mymoorapelta had fleshy, muscular tongues that could assist in feeding on low-growing plants, while related nodosaurids had fleshy cheeks and cheek plates that covered tooth rows for defense and to prevent food loss while eating.
Direct evidence of tooth occlusion has not been preserved in Mymoorapelta.
Mymoorapelta appears adapted for open environments due to competition with diplodocid sauropods.

Reconstructions by Coombs in 1978 suggest Mymoorapelta's forelimbs bore most of its weight and were adapted for high force delivery, possibly for food gathering, though their hoof-like manus would have limited fossorial capabilities.

While the tail was thought to be used for defense against predators, recent findings suggest it might have been used for intraspecific combat, a possibility that might apply to basal taxa like Mymoorapelta.
The clade Nodosauridae was named in 1890 by Othniel Charles Marsh, who designated Nodosaurus as the type genus, and the genus Mymoorapelta was named by Kirkland and Carpenter in 1994.
Mymoorapelta maysi is the only known species in the extinct genus Mymoorapelta.

It is debated whether Mymoorapelta may be an ankylosaur outside both Nodosauridae and Ankylosauridae, and there is currently some controversy regarding the position of this ankylosaurian within Ankylosauria.

Mymoorapelta lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 155 to 150 million years ago, and nodosaurids first evolved in the Late Jurassic (ca. 155 mya), with Mymoorapelta being an early member of this evolutionary radiation.

Mymoorapelta lived during the late Jurassic period, approximately 150 to 145 million years ago, in the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian stages, and has a limited known distribution found at two sites in Western Colorado, plus the Hanksville-Burpee and potential Albuquerque specimens.
It is debated whether an osteoderm from New Mexico belongs to Mymoorapelta, as it is morphologically similar but stratigraphically closer to Gargoyleosaurus.
Researchers suggest that category 1 sacral shields might represent a growth stage of category 2 shields, similar to traits seen in modern armadillos and alligators.
